hints: List the ions present in each aqueous electrolyte, remembering water provides $\text{H}^{+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ in addition to the solute ions.
At the cathode compare the cations, a very reactive metal ion stays in solution and $\text{H}_{2}$ is formed, while a less reactive metal like copper is discharged.
At the anode compare $\text{OH}^{-}$ with halide ions, dilute chloride gives $\text{O}_{2}$ but concentrated chloride gives $\text{Cl}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Sort out what can move to each electrode**
Think of it like a race. Negative ions go to the positive anode, positive ions go to the negative cathode. In aqueous solutions you always have $\text{H}^{+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ from water as well as the ions from the salt, base or acid.

Decide the cathode product**
At the cathode, the ion that is easier to reduce is discharged. $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ are very reactive metals, much harder to reduce than water, so $\text{H}^{+}$ / water is reduced: $2\text{H}^{+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}$. $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is below hydrogen in reactivity, so copper metal is deposited: $\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}$.

Decide the anode product using concentration**
At the anode, $\text{OH}^{-}$ competes with other anions. With $\text{NaOH}$ there is only $\text{OH}^{-}$, so $\text{O}_{2}$ is liberated. With dilute $\text{CuCl}_{2}$, $\text{Cl}^{-}$ is dilute so $\text{OH}^{-}$ is preferentially discharged to give $\text{O}_{2}$. With concentrated $\text{MgCl}_{2}$, the high $\text{Cl}^{-}$ concentration means $\text{Cl}^{-}$ is discharged to give $\text{Cl}_{2}$: $2\text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cl}_{2} + 2\text{e}^{-}$.

Final answer: $\text{NaOH(aq)}$: anode $\text{O}_{2}$, cathode $\text{H}_{2}$
dilute $\text{CuCl}_{2}\text{(aq)}$: anode $\text{O}_{2}$, cathode $\text{Cu}$
concentrated $\text{MgCl}_{2}\text{(aq)}$: anode $\text{Cl}_{2}$, cathode $\text{H}_{2}$

hints: Identify the only two ions present in molten $\text{ZnBr}_{2}$, $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ and $\text{Br}^{-}$, and match them to cathode (reduction) and anode (oxidation).
Recall OILRIG, oxidation is loss of electrons at the anode, reduction is gain of electrons at the cathode.
Balance charge and atoms in each half-equation, bromide needs 2 ions to make $\text{Br}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Picture the molten liquid**
Molten means no water, just mobile ions. $\text{ZnBr}_{2}$ gives $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ which is attracted to the negative cathode, and $\text{Br}^{-}$ which is attracted to the positive anode. That already tells you where each reaction happens.

Write the two half-equations**
At the anode, bromide loses electrons to form bromine molecules: $$2\text{Br}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Br}_{2} + 2\text{e}^{-}$$ At the cathode, zinc ions gain electrons to form zinc atoms: $$\text{Zn}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Zn}$$ Check balance, atoms and charge balance on both sides.

Label oxidation and reduction**
Loss of electrons is oxidation, so $\text{Br}^{-}$ is oxidised. Gain of electrons is reduction, so $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ is reduced. Together they make the whole electrolysis a redox process, electrons lost at one electrode equal electrons gained at the other.

Final answer: Anode: $2\text{Br}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Br}_{2} + 2\text{e}^{-}$
Cathode: $\text{Zn}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Zn}$
$\text{Br}^{-}$ is oxidised (loss of electrons) and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ is reduced (gain of electrons).

hints: Think what the products look like, $\text{Br}_{2}$ as a coloured vapour and $\text{Zn}$ as a silvery liquid metal.
walkthrough:
Translate chemistry into what you would see**
Describe, do not name the theory. Bromine is a very distinctive orange-brown vapour, seen fuming at the anode. Alternatively you would see a silvery grey liquid of molten zinc collecting at the cathode. Either visible change earns credit.
Final answer: Orange-brown vapour forms at the anode (or grey silvery liquid zinc forms at the cathode).

hints: Start with $Q = It$, convert 50.0 minutes to seconds before multiplying by 1.20 A.
Convert charge to moles of electrons using $n(\text{e}^{-}) = Q / 96500$, then use the cathode half-equation $2\text{H}^{+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}$ to find moles of $\text{H}_{2}$.
Convert moles of gas to volume using $24000 \text{ cm}^{3} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ under room conditions.
walkthrough:
Find the total charge passed**
Charge links current and time: $$Q = It$$ Time must be in seconds: $$t = 50.0 \times 60 = 3000 \text{ s}$$ So: $$Q = 1.20 \times 3000 = 3600 \text{ C}$$

Convert charge to moles of electrons then to moles of hydrogen**
One Faraday, $96500 \text{ C}$, is one mole of electrons: $$n(\text{e}^{-}) = \frac{3600}{96500} = 0.0373 \text{ mol}$$ At the cathode in dilute acid, hydrogen is formed: $$2\text{H}^{+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{H}_{2}$$ Two moles of electrons give one mole of $\text{H}_{2}$: $$n(\text{H}_{2}) = \frac{0.0373}{2} = 0.01865 \text{ mol}$$

Convert moles to volume**
Under room conditions one mole of gas occupies $24000 \text{ cm}^{3}$: $$V = n \times 24000$$ $$V = 0.01865 \times 24000 = 448 \text{ cm}^{3}$$ This is the maximum cathode volume, hydrogen, twice the anode oxygen volume.
